name: John
primary_meaning: John is a masculine name of Hebrew origin, from Yôḥānān (יוֹחָנָן), meaning “God has been gracious”. It owes its popularity to two saints — John the Baptist and the apostle John — and for centuries was the most common male name in the English-speaking world.
meaning_explanation: Yôḥānān is a theophoric name: Yô- is a short form of God's name and ḥānan means “to be gracious”. It passed into Greek as Iōannēs, Latin Ioannes/Johannes, Old French Jehan and Middle English Iohn/John.

etymology.morphology: Theophoric compound: Yô (God) + ḥānan, “has been gracious”; long form Yəhôḥānān.
etymology.explanation: From Hebrew Yôḥānān / Yəhôḥānān via Greek Ἰωάννης and Latin Ioannes, Johannes.
etymology.false_etymology_warning: Jonathan (Yonatan, “given by God”) is a different name and not related to John.

origin.explanation: Hebrew, through Greek and Latin. It was a favourite among the Greeks and spread across Europe after the First Crusade; Middle English had Iohn, Ihon, Jan by the 12th century.

religion.association: Christian — John the Baptist and John the Apostle
religion.status: New Testament name of two major saints
religion.explanation: John the Baptist baptised Jesus; John the Apostle is traditionally regarded as the author of the Gospel of John. The name was also taken by many popes, patriarchs, emperors and kings.

biblical.verse_reference: Gospel of John; Matthew 3 (John the Baptist)
biblical.note: Also borne by minor figures in the Old Testament.

saint.saint_name: Saint John the Baptist; Saint John the Apostle
saint.note: Two of the most venerated saints in Christianity.

cultural.meaning: Jack began as a nickname for John and is now a name in its own right.
cultural.impact: In the Second Temple period Yohanan was the fifth most popular male name among Jews in Judaea.

items: Borne by the high priest Johanan (fl. 407 BC) and King John Hyrcanus (d. 104 BC).
Spread through Europe after the First Crusade.
history.person: John the Baptist and John the Apostle (1st century).

modern_usage: John was the most popular name for baby boys in the United States until 1924 and was still 20th in 2006; by 2004 it had left the top 50 in England and Wales.
variant_notes: Ian (Scottish), Sean (Irish), Juan (Spanish), Jean (French), Giovanni (Italian), Johannes (German, Latin), Ivan (Slavic); Jack and Johnny are English pet forms.

faq.a: “God has been gracious”, from the Hebrew Yôḥānān.
Yes — John the Baptist and John the Apostle in the New Testament, plus minor Old Testament figures.

faq.q: Are John and Jonathan the same name?
faq.a: No. Jonathan comes from Yonatan, “given by God”, and is not etymologically related.

faq.q: Why is Jack a nickname for John?
faq.a: Jack developed in Middle English as a pet form of John and is now an independent name.

faq.q: What is John in other languages?
faq.a: Juan (Spanish), Jean (French), Giovanni (Italian), Johannes (German), Ivan (Russian), Sean (Irish), Ian (Scottish).
